groups.title: Read an Academic Passage
groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.context:
A habit is a behavior that a person performs almost automatically, with little conscious thought. Brushing one's teeth, locking the door, and checking a phone on waking are familiar examples. Psychologists describe a habit as a loop with three parts: a cue that triggers the behavior, the routine itself, and a reward that makes the brain want to repeat it.

Habits form through repetition in a stable setting. Each time a routine follows the same cue and brings a reward, the link between them grows stronger, until the cue alone is enough to start the action. This takes longer than many people assume. In one well-known study at a London university, volunteers needed about two months, on average, before a new daily behavior felt automatic, and some needed far longer. Missing a single day, however, did not noticeably slow their progress.

Because habits are tied to cues, they are hard to break by willpower alone. An old routine tends to return whenever the familiar cue appears, especially when a person is tired or under stress. For this reason, psychologists often advise changing the surroundings instead: keeping snacks out of sight, for instance, or taking a different route home. Research on people who have just moved suggests the same thing. In a new place, the old cues are missing, so old routines are easier to replace.

groups.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
groups.context:
In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from a holiday to find that mold had grown on one of the dishes in which he was raising bacteria. Around the mold, the bacteria had died. Fleming named the substance responsible penicillin, but he could not produce enough of it to treat patients. That step was taken more than a decade later by a team at Oxford that included Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, and by the mid-1940s factories were turning out the drug in enormous quantities.

Penicillin transformed medicine. Infections that had often been fatal could now be cured within days. Yet Fleming himself sounded a warning. Accepting the Nobel Prize in 1945, he pointed out that careless use of the drug might allow bacteria to become resistant to it.

His fear proved justified. In any large population of bacteria, a few may happen to carry a trait that lets them survive a drug. When an antibiotic kills their competitors, these survivors multiply and pass the trait on. The more widely antibiotics are used, therefore, the more chances resistant strains have to spread. Today some infections no longer respond to drugs that once cured them easily, and few new antibiotics have reached the market in recent decades. The discovery that seemed to defeat bacterial disease turned out to be only the opening move in a much longer contest.

options: Ways of reducing the movement of tall buildings in wind
Reasons why modern towers are taller than older ones
The history of the world's most famous skyscrapers
How engineers measure the speed of the wind

questions.explanation: After explaining that towers sway, the professor asks 'how do they do it?' and gives two answers: shape and weight.

listening.script: Here's something that might surprise you. If you stand at the top of a very tall building on a windy day, the floor under your feet is moving. Skyscrapers sway. The very tallest can move a meter or more in a storm, and they're designed to. A tower that can bend a little is actually safer than one that can't. So the real problem for engineers isn't keeping the building up. It's keeping the people inside comfortable, because nobody wants to feel seasick at their desk. So, how do they do it? One answer is shape. When wind flows around a square tower, it breaks into swirls of air that push the building from side to side. Rounded corners, or an outline that changes as the tower rises, break up those swirls before they get strong. The Burj Khalifa in Dubai does exactly that. Its outline keeps changing on the way up, so the wind never gets organized. A second answer is weight. Near the top of Taipei 101, in Taiwan, there's an enormous steel ball, more than six hundred tons of it, hanging from cables. When the wind pushes the tower one way, the ball swings the other way and absorbs much of the movement. And it isn't hidden. Visitors can go and look at it. For next time, I'd like each of you to find one more building that uses a trick like this.

options: Why wheat became the most important crop in Europe
How medieval villages shared their farmland
How farm animals were kept alive through the winter
Why farmers change the crop grown in a field

questions.explanation: The topic is named at the start, 'crop rotation', and the talk explains why it works and how it improved.

listening.script: Today's topic is a farming idea that's thousands of years old and still in use: crop rotation. The idea is simple. You don't grow the same crop in the same field year after year. Why not? Well, think about what happens if you plant wheat again and again. Wheat takes a lot of nitrogen out of the soil, so each harvest gets a little smaller. And the insects and diseases that like wheat stay right there in the field, waiting for next year's meal. Now, farmers long ago knew nothing about nitrogen, but they could see the results. In medieval Europe, many villages divided their land into three big fields, and each year one of the three was left empty to rest. It worked. But notice the cost. A third of the land grew nothing. The real breakthrough, which spread across England in the seventeen hundreds, was a four-year rotation. Two of the years were for grain. In the other two, farmers grew turnips and clover. No resting year at all. How was that possible? Clover belongs to the same family as peas and beans, and bacteria living on the roots of these plants take nitrogen from the air and put it back into the soil. So the clover was feeding the field. And the turnips and clover also fed the farm animals through the winter, which meant more animals and more manure for the soil. More food from the same land. Not bad for a simple change of plan.

answers: Part of the land produced no food each year.

options: How linguists count the world's languages

listening.script: There are roughly seven thousand languages spoken in the world today. By the end of this century, by many estimates, around half of them will have fallen silent. Now, I want to be careful here, because people tend to picture this the wrong way. Languages rarely die because their speakers die. They die because parents, usually for perfectly sensible reasons, stop passing them on. If the language of school, of work, of the city is something else, then speaking that other language to your children looks like giving them a head start. Nobody decides to kill a language. It just isn't handed down. And one generation is all it takes. So what, you might say. Wouldn't life be simpler with fewer languages? Well, consider what goes with them. A community that has lived in one place for centuries has names for plants, for animals, for kinds of weather, that often exist nowhere else and were never written down. In New Zealand in the nineteen eighties, Māori communities began running preschools, called language nests, where small children heard nothing but Māori all day. The idea has since been copied elsewhere, including Hawaii. It doesn't guarantee survival. But it does show that the decline is not a law of nature.

And for us linguists, every language is a piece of evidence about what the human mind can do. Lose it, and that evidence is gone for good. It isn't hopeless, though. In New Zealand in the nineteen eighties, Māori communities began running preschools, called language nests, where small children heard nothing but Māori all day. The idea has since been copied elsewhere, including Hawaii. It doesn't guarantee survival. But it does show that the decline is not a law of nature.

questions.prompt: Write an email to Ms. Okonkwo. Write as much as you can and in complete sentences.

Dear Ms. Okonkwo,

I am writing because I left something behind in Whitlock Hall yesterday. I attended the public lecture on city gardens, which ended at about 8:30 p.m. When I got home, I realized that my jacket was missing. I went back at once, but the building was already locked.

The jacket is dark green with a gray hood. I was sitting in the fourth row of the lecture hall, near the left aisle, and I believe I hung it over the back of my seat. My house keys are in the inside pocket, on a red key ring, so I am anxious to find it.

Could you please tell me whether the jacket has been handed in? If it has, when and where could I collect it? I can come to the building at any time today or tomorrow, and I will bring my student card.

groups.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
groups.instructions: Your professor is teaching a class on public health. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

professor.name: Dr. Halvorsen
professor.post: This week we are studying how governments try to influence what people eat and drink. Dozens of countries, including Mexico and the United Kingdom, now place a special tax on sugary drinks. Supporters argue that higher prices lead people to consume less sugar and that the money can pay for health programs. Critics reply that such taxes fall hardest on families with low incomes and that people should be free to choose. What is your view? Should governments tax sugary drinks? Why or why not?

students.name: Renata
students.post: I support the tax. When something costs more, people buy less of it, and that is especially true of teenagers, who have little money of their own. A tax also pushes companies to put less sugar in their products so that they pay less. A small change in price seems to me an easy way to protect children.

students.name: Callum
students.post: I don't think a tax is the right tool. Rich people will hardly notice a few extra cents, so the cost falls mostly on poorer families. Besides, people can simply switch to other sweet foods. I would rather see governments spend money on education and on free drinking water in every school.

questions.prompt: Express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
questions.explanation:
Model response:

I believe governments should tax sugary drinks, but only if the tax is designed carefully. Callum is right that a higher price is harder on families with little money. However, those same families often suffer most from the health problems connected with too much sugar, so they also have the most to gain. To make the policy fair, the money collected should go back to the communities that pay it, for example by lowering the price of fruit and vegetables or by putting free water fountains in public places. I would also add an idea that has not been mentioned: the tax could depend on the amount of sugar in each drink rather than on the size of the bottle. Then companies would have a strong reason to change their recipes, and people could keep buying their favorite brands in a healthier form.

stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: One friend I don't see very often is Mateo. We met on the first day of high school, because the teacher gave us seats next to each other. We soon discovered that we supported the same football team, and after that we spent almost every weekend together. Two years ago, he moved to another city to study engineering, so now we mostly keep in touch online. We send each other short voice messages a few times a week, usually about football or something funny that happened. About once a month we have a long video call, and during the holidays we always try to meet in person.

listening.script: Thank you for joining me today. I'd like to start with your own experience. Think of a friend you don't see very often. How did the two of you meet, and how do you stay in contact now?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 2 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I definitely prefer having a few close friends. For me, friendship takes time, and I only have a limited amount of it because of my studies and my part-time job. If I tried to stay close to twenty people, I would not be able to give any of them real attention. With my three best friends, I can talk about serious things, such as family problems or worries about the future, and I know they will listen. Of course, I enjoy meeting new people in class, and I am friendly with many of them. But I would call them acquaintances rather than true friends.

listening.script: Some people like to have a large circle of friends, while others prefer just a few close ones. Which is closer to your own preference, and why?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 3 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I disagree with that view. Distance certainly makes a friendship harder, because you cannot share everyday moments, like eating lunch together. However, I think the strength of a friendship depends on effort, not on location. My cousin and her best friend have lived in different countries for ten years, and they are still very close because they call each other every Sunday. In some ways, distance can even improve a friendship, since people stop taking each other for granted. On the other hand, if neither person makes time for the other, the friendship will fade, even if they live on the same street.

listening.script: Now I'd like to hear your opinion. Some people believe that a friendship cannot really stay strong when two friends live far away from each other. Do you agree or disagree? Why?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 4 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I think universities should do more, although students also have to make an effort. Starting university can be very lonely, especially for students who come from another city or country and know nobody. Loneliness affects their health and their grades, so it is in the university's interest to help. For example, universities could organize small group activities in the first weeks, such as hiking trips or cooking evenings, instead of only big welcome parties where shy people feel lost. They could also match each new student with an older student from the same department. After that first step, it is up to the students to keep the friendships going.

listening.script: Here is my last question. Many students move to a new city for university and find it hard to make friends there. Do you think universities should do more to help new students build friendships, or is that the students' own responsibility? Please explain.
